summary: A route to a known result, not found in the literature searched: MOND's 'simple' interpolating function, nu = 1/2 + (1/4 + a0/g_N)^(1/2), whose boost at g_N = a0 is the golden ratio, follows exactly from the same curve that traces the cosmic expansion, given two stated inputs. The function itself is not new (Famaey and Binney 2005), and it has recently been obtained approximately by a different route, from the cosmic and Rindler horizons (Urueña Palomo 2026); the route through the expansion history's own curve was not found in the literature searched. The curve: for a flat universe of matter and a constant push, the square root of the matter fraction traces a tractrix; if Omega_m = 1/pi, its leash stands at 55.65 degrees from the vertical today. McGaugh's galaxy law can be written on the same curve. The two inputs are the boost read off the curve and the postulate that a galaxy is placed on the curve by the same rule as the universe. Both inputs were taken up after the fact, and a0 is imposed, so the note records a conditional derivation, not a prediction. Omega_m = 1/pi is the programme's preregistered value; it was published earlier by another author and chosen when Omega_m of about 0.31 was known (see the programme overview). Other earlier work cited: Pazy and Argaman 2012, and Milgrom 1999 and 2009. Further exact readings, found after the fact, are given: - the involute pair, catenary and tractrix, whose squared heights are pi and 1/pi today; - the rim of the pseudosphere (the circle where its two halves meet) as the Big Bang; this is not the force-balance 'rim' of the deposited rim note r3b; - the observed, Newtonian and memory fields as the growing, full and decaying modes; - the equation g (g - g_N) = a0 g_N, which is equivalent to the law and derives nothing. An open ambiguity, stated after these notes were frozen: where the Big Bang sits on the hyperbolic horn. In this note the curve plots the height sqrt(Omega_m), which is 1 at the Big Bang, so the Big Bang falls on the widest circle (the rim), and the surface narrows toward the de Sitter end state. The companion note 'A dictionary between a 4D-fall cosmology and the mod-210 prime corpus: zeros as resonances of a postulated cusp at the Big Bang rim' (deposited on Zenodo alongside this one) instead postulates the Big Bang at the cusp of the modular surface, where the closed circles shrink to nothing. The author's view, which he says he has always held, is the cusp: the Big Bang starts at the cusp, a point, as general relativity reduces the universe to a point, and the mirror history (the author's origin ruling) joins ours there. One reading, offered by the drafter (Claude) and not by the author, is that the one-curve rim then marks the starting value of the matter fraction rather than a size. None of this is derived or tested, and the notes are not revised for it. Two tests designed before computing found, as expected, no system in the picture that supplies the modes or the placement. A consistency check on SPARC data (already used) finds the simple function indistinguishable from McGaugh's: a0 is 1.11 vs 1.14 e-10 m/s^2, and the scatter is 0.131 dex for both. Solar-system limits from Cassini apply to modified-gravity MOND, not to this model. The author has adopted the simple function as the galaxy law of the model (version r7f, not deposited), with a0 unchanged at 1.2e-10 m/s^2. The note makes no prediction. It was drafted with Claude (Anthropic) and reviewed by independent sessions of the same model.
title: One curve at two scales: the tractrix of the cosmic expansion and of the galaxy law

summary: This academic curriculum module delivers an analytical, physical, and computational exposition of satellite technology, Keplerian orbital mechanics, communications link budgets, and spacecraft subsystems across Low Earth Orbit (LEO), Medium Earth Orbit (MEO), and Geostationary Earth Orbit (GEO) environments. Key Technical Topics & Curricular Areas Covered: 1. Orbital Mechanics & Mission Design: Circular velocity derivations (v = sqrt(mu/r)), Kepler's Third Law orbital period determinations, Geostationary altitude sizing, and two-impulse Hohmann transfer delta-v maneuvers. 2. Space Communications & RF Link Budgets: Free-space path loss (FSPL) formulations across C-band, Ku-band, and Ka-band frequencies; antenna gain trade-offs; receiver noise figure thresholds; and rain fade atmospheric attenuation. 3. Satellite Subsystems Architecture: Attitude Determination and Control Systems (ADCS) using reaction wheels and magnetorquers; space power systems utilizing photovoltaic arrays and battery storage under orbital eclipse cycling; and thermal management via radiators and multi-layer insulation (MLI). 4. Modern Computational & AI-Era Paradigms: Machine-learning-augmented orbital perturbation propagators (ML-SGP4) correcting for solar-storm atmospheric drag surges; deep reinforcement learning for autonomous in-orbit collision avoidance; and edge AI hyperspectral compression on space-grade FPGAs. 5. Contemporary Systems Engineering Trade-offs: LEO mega-constellations vs. GEO wide-area platforms, optical inter-satellite links (ISLs) vs. RF ground relays, electric Hall-effect thrusters vs. chemical monopropellants, and standardized CubeSat modularity vs. high-reliability radiation-hardened redundancy. 6. Relativistic Physics in Space Systems: Gravitational time dilation and special relativity corrections essential for sub-meter Global Navigation Satellite Systems (GNSS). 7. Pedagogical Features: An interactive web-based orbit velocity and orbital period calculator with dynamic trajectory visualization, structured conceptual reviews, and step-by-step worked numerical engineering problems with explicit physical units. Format: Open Educational Resource (OER) prepared for persistent archiving on Zenodo and indexing in MERLOT. Permanent Webpage URL: https://prep4uni.online/stem/physical-technologies/aerospace-and-aeronautical-engineering/satellite-technology/

summary: We present the AI Safety Formalization Atlas (AISFA), an open Lean 4 library and ledger that together form a shared epistemic infrastructure for AI safety mathematics: a record of what is proved, from which hypotheses and against which source, with rules for what may enter it. The Atlas has three aims. It formalizes AI safety results that often start as informal arguments. Where it can, it strengthens them, usually by proving them over wider classes of objects or under weaker hypotheses, and occasionally with sharper conclusions. It makes these very different results interoperable, so that they can be composed and a result proved in one domain can be transferred to another. We describe it to invite collaborators. The library holds about 200,000 lines of kernel-checked Lean. AI coding agents wrote the Atlas’s own Lean, and people check the critical points. Each statement that transcribes a published claim is graded against its printed wording: of 316 graded, 201 are stated more generally than print, and eighteen printed claims in twelve sources proved false as printed, each refuted in Lean beside a proved repair. One knowability interface carries impossibility results of one shape across six domains. As a public verifier for nine community solutions to Math for AI Safety open problems, the Atlas checked four, found three partial and two conditional.  Repository: https://github.com/mbrcic/ai-safety-formalization-atlas. Site: https://mbrcic.github.io/ai-safety-formalization-atlas/
title: The AI Safety Formalization Atlas: a machine-checked memory for AI safety mathematics

summary: This work introduces Theorem 81 — Constitutive Closure of Cosmological Expansion , developed within the Trinamica CP364 framework, with the aim of establishing a mathematical connection between elastic time dynamics and cosmological evolution. The research forms part of the CP364 scientific programme and constitutes a mathematical extension of the dossier HUBBLE CP364 — Foundations of Trinamica and Active Time Dynamics (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.20666751). Theorem 81 introduces a constitutive structure in which elastic temporal deformation, active energy, temporal tension, coherence, and process memory contribute to defining the dynamic state of the system and its cosmological evolution. The formalization integrates three fundamental levels: Constitutive level: elastic temporal deformation, active energy, tension, and coherence. Dynamic level: Transition Regime (RT), elastic temporal memory, coupling, and process dynamics. Cosmological level: constitutive scale function, Hubble parameter, and connection with cosmological observables. The work distinguishes two levels of mathematical formalization: Theorem 81A — Conditional Kinematic Closure Establishes the conditions under which a positive and differentiable constitutive function of the trinamical state can represent the cosmological scale factor and yield the expansion parameter through its logarithmic derivative with respect to cosmic time. Problem 81B — Dynamic Constitutive Closure Defines the mathematical programme required to determine the cosmological constitutive function through CP364 evolution laws, RT–TEC compatibility, dynamic coupling, initial conditions, and process memory. The formalization includes: The distinction between elastic time, the evolutionary parameter of the Transition Regime, and cosmic time. The mathematical connection between the Transition Regime (RT) and the Trinamical Field Equations (TEC). The relationship between active energy, deformation, and elastic temporal tension. The introduction of an elastic response with a saturation function. The differential formalization of temporal coherence. The integration of elastic temporal memory into constitutive dynamics. The distinction between tensional decay, observational variation, and dynamic coupling. The definition of a candidate family of CP364 cosmological models. The formulation of the expansion parameter H_CP364(t) and its connection with H_CP364(z). The connection with redshift, luminosity distance, and distance modulus. The conditions for existence, regularity, saturation, and transitions between different evolutionary branches. The central contribution of Theorem 81 lies in the construction of a mathematical bridge between the internal dynamics of the Φ domain and the cosmological representation of expansion, while maintaining an explicit distinction between local constitutive quantities, process dynamics, and cosmological observables. From this perspective, cosmological expansion is investigated as a possible manifestation of a structural process in which temporal deformation, energy, coherence, and memory contribute to the evolution of the system. summary: These supplementary materials accompany a PhD thesis investigating the use of large language models (LLMs) for automated export-control compliance screening in UK universities. The research examines LLM-based classification, regulatory information retrieval, explainability, and the evaluation of compliance-support systems. The record contains two supplementary documents: Supplementary Material S1: Fine-Tuning Methodology and Supporting Analyses S1 provides additional methodological documentation, including fine-tuning configurations, implementation details, worked examples, and supporting reference material for the export-control screening system. Supplementary Material S2: ECIR Retrieval Evaluation Data and Reproducibility S2 documents the evaluation of regulatory information retrieval, including the relevance-judgement protocol, retrieval configurations, evaluation measures, aggregate results, and methodological limitations. Together, these documents provide additional information supporting the methods and findings presented in the doctoral thesis. They are intended to facilitate transparency, scholarly scrutiny, and reproducibility. Data availability: This record contains two supplementary PDF documents and an accompanying ZIP archive of supporting ECIR retrieval-evaluation materials. The archive includes evaluation data, relevance judgements, methodological documentation, and supporting analysis files. The export control officer has authorised the public release of her individual relevance judgements under the applicable licence.

direction_title: Memory Cortex: new source-grounded retrieval and continual-memory research [FORWARD]
summary: Being • Becoming • Beyond the Classroom The title of the conference proposes a sequence and a challenge. Being asks who our students are before formal education begins: their languages, memories, families, social relationships, intellectual curiosity and sense of dignity. Becoming asks what education makes possible: learning, confidence, judgment, competence, agency and the courage to imagine alternative futures. Beyond the Classroom asks where those capacities will be exercised. The answer must include the home, the village, the market, the workplace, public institutions and the natural environment. The Santal Parganas region is an especially meaningful setting for this conversation. The six districts of Dumka, Deoghar, Godda, Jamtara, Pakur and Sahibganj are home to many communities and languages, including strong Santal traditions of land, social life, artistic expression and collective memory. Young people in the region encounter the opportunities of higher education alongside economic and geographical obstacles: variable transport access, family responsibilities, limited availability of some courses, digital connectivity and language differences. A regional conference therefore cannot define educational progress only in terms of examination results or numbers enrolled. It must ask whether students can remain in education, learn well, exercise genuine choice and carry their skills into forms of work and citizenship that they themselves value. A degree is significant, but its meaning is diminished if acquiring it requires a student to abandon all confidence in the community from which they come. The conference’s central proposition Education becomes socially transformative when it enlarges human capability while respecting cultural inheritance, promoting critical inquiry and strengthening responsibility for other persons and the environment. The papers in this book test that proposition in different ways, from Indigenous knowledge and climate justice to AI, conflict prevention, women’s participation, entrepreneurship, educational continuity and language learning

summary: Unrefereed research candidate. Several forecasters each give a probability for the same yes/no event (rain tomorrow, a patient relapsing, an election). Each has seen different evidence and reports honestly. The best combination is the probability of the event given all the reports together, but that depends on how the forecasters' evidence overlaps, which is unknown. An aggregator has to learn it from a track record of past cases with known outcomes. This paper asks how long that track record must be. What was known. Lin and Chen (NeurIPS 2023) set up the model: n experts, each with at most m possible signals, exact calibrated reports, and T past cases. For experts whose evidence is independent given the outcome they showed that between about log(1/δ)/ε and 1/ε 2 cases are needed for accuracy ε; for arbitrary dependence, between about m n−2 /ε and m n /ε 2 . They conjectured that 1/ε is the right dependence and asked about the middle ground. Under conditional independence the ideal combination is the classical multiplicative pooling formula (their Lemma 5.1, credited to Bordley). Main result. Let η bound the conditional total correlation of the reports given the outcome: how much the experts share beyond what each knows about the outcome. With failure probability δ ≤ 1/32, the minimax excess Brier risk is of order min{1, log(1/δ)/T + min(η, m n /T)}, up to universal constants. So about log(1/δ)/ε cases are needed and suffice for conditionally independent experts, and about (m n + log(1/δ))/ε under arbitrary dependence, which raises the earlier m n−2 lower bound to m n . One estimator attains the rate without knowing η: fit the pooling formula, fit a lookup table, and keep whichever does better on held-out cases. The hard examples keep every expert's calibration curve, the prior and the whole distribution of report vectors fixed, so the difficulty lies in interactions that no single expert's track record reveals. Further results: the rate when the prior is known, impossibility of uniform consistency with unbounded report alphabets under any fixed dependence allowance, and an extension to finitely many outcomes. Relation to standard tools. For conditionally independent experts, localised-complexity arguments already give the upper bound up to a factor log T; the new parts there are removing that factor and the matching lower bounds. The main new content is the dependence trade-off and the calibrated worst-case construction. Limits. Reports are exact, honest, calibrated posteriors; rounding to whole percentages is not covered. The bounds are worst case over all laws (a particular group of forecasters may be much easier) and the constants are not optimised. With k outcomes, a factor of about k between the upper and lower bounds remains open. Contents. The paper (LaTeX source and PDF); an exact-arithmetic verification script for the finite algebra of the constructions (9075 checks, standard library) and a small illustrative simulation, with their recorded outputs; the bibliography, a machine-readable index, a research-gate record, a review summary, a replay receipt and SHA-256 sums. Every check exits with an error on failure, also under python -O. Assurance. Written proofs; the scripts check finite algebra only. Internal AI-assisted review only: a combined five-role Claude review, the lead's exact checks with a negative control and a small simulation, one revision round, then a re-review and a proof audit of the new and rewritten proofs. summary: Analysis code and derived results supporting Neurophotonics manuscript NPH-260158-1. The primary benchmark evaluates recovery of paired HbO/HbR responses injected in optical density before preprocessing into resting-state recordings. The archive includes participant-level estimates, preprocessing calibration, both denominator grids, active-channel-fraction and HbR-delay sensitivity analyses, event-timing checks, task-data descriptors, and a separate HbO synthetic experiment. The record contains NPH-260158-1_Code_and_Results.zip and NPH-260158-1_Supplementary_Tables.xlsx. Reproduction instructions and source data links are provided in README.md within the ZIP. The XLSX file contains the results worksheets cited in the manuscript. Original recordings are not included. Version 1.2.3 adds a matched MULPA benchmark without TDDR in all 57 participants, at three doses, for both chromophores and all 11 estimators. Scripts, participant outputs, tables, environment information and validation are in verification/tddr_ablation. The TDDR diagnostic in all 85 resting recordings, task-off fractions and demographic checks remain in verification/response_alignment. Primary estimates, earlier sensitivity outputs, figures and the companion workbook are unchanged from version 1.2.2. summary: Overview ChaosFlow is a configuration-driven research platform for evaluating fault recovery, operational resilience, and data integrity in distributed Big Data pipelines integrating Apache Kafka, Apache Spark Structured Streaming, Apache Hadoop HDFS, and Docker. This research dataset documents controlled fault-injection experiments investigating the distinction between infrastructure recovery, service readiness, application progress, sustained-throughput recovery, and independently verified output correctness. Experimental Design The experimental protocol covers eight scenarios: C0: No Fault C1: Kafka Container Stop C2: Kafka Container Restart C3: Spark Worker Failure C4: HDFS DataNode Failure C5: Network Fault C6: Storage Pressure C7: Checkpoint-Related Fault Each scenario is evaluated under observer-enabled and observer-disabled configurations, with 15 qualifying repetitions per experimental cell. The primary campaign records 240 qualifying observations and 16 additional invalid attempts. The broader research includes an independently executed second-machine evaluation, documented in the corresponding experimental evidence. Dataset and Correctness Verification The experimental workload consists of 1,000,000 input records, yielding 966,002 expected output occurrences after deterministic cleaning and filtering. Data correctness is assessed through independent schema-aware typed-row multiset verification and production validation. The research distinguishes successful qualifying executions from invalid attempts, including fault-exposed executions with incomplete output. Research Objectives The evidence supports investigation of: Differences between infrastructure, service, application, and throughput recovery. Data correctness following infrastructure fault injection. Monitoring and observer overhead. Recovery measurement sensitivity and censored observations. Experimental reproducibility across physical computing environments. Limitations of container-health indicators as evidence of application and data recovery. Research Artifacts The deposited materials provide the available experimental records, correctness-validation evidence, recovery measurements, statistical analyses, and supporting audit documentation included in this release. The dataset is intended to support independent research verification, reproducibility, and further investigation of distributed data-pipeline resilience. Limitations The reported findings are conditional on the specified experimental topology, workload, qualification criteria, and recovery-measurement definitions. Qualifying-run correctness does not imply unconditional correctness across all execution attempts.

summary: This repository holds the reference Python implementation of TRUST-Balance (Trustworthy Risk-adaptive Utility and STructure-preserving Balancing), a model-agnostic framework for imbalanced classification. TRUST-Balance treats class-imbalance handling as risk-constrained intervention selection rather than fixed resampling. It splits the minority class into regions with K-means. For each region it chooses between screened synthetic generation, localised reweighting and abstention, scoring each candidate by its estimated reduction in class-balanced validation risk. That score is penalised for uncertainty, structural distortion and cost, and is subject to a tolerance on majority-class loss. The procedure stops when no intervention gives a positive utility. The estimator is scikit-learn compatible and works with any probabilistic classifier. It has three optional modes: a post-selection refit (TRUST+R), a Hoeffding-type acceptance certificate (TRUST-C), and subsampled screening that scales to millions of records. The archive contains the estimator and re-implementations of three recent adaptive baselines (ART, UGO and GDEO). It also includes a script that downloads the 27 public benchmark datasets from KEEL, PMLB/UCI and scikit-learn, plus the full experimental pipeline. The pipeline benchmarks logistic regression, random forests and XGBoost against 13 competing approaches, including the unmodified model. It also runs ablation, safeguard stress tests, sensitivity, robustness to imbalance ratio, label noise and class overlap, multiclass extension, certification and scalability studies up to one million records. The archive also ships the raw per-run results as CSV, the summary tables, the figures, and analysis scripts that reproduce every table and figure of the accompanying article. Those statistics include Friedman/Iman–Davenport tests, Nemenyi critical differences and Holm-corrected Wilcoxon tests. Code is released under the MIT licence and results under CC BY 4.0. summary: Abstract: Background: The number of children experiencing postnatal situations of neurological risk (such as psycho-motor developmental disorders and delays) after birth has increased in recent years. These infants often require multiple pediatric interventions to address functional problems that might generate stress, anxiety, and discomfort. The aim of the present study is to determine whether the level of salivary cortisol, as a stress marker, increases after hydrotherapy and landbased therapy in children at risk of or currently presenting delayed psycho-motor development. Methods: Saliva samples were collected from 25 children (aged 3–36 months) between June 2022 and January 2023 at the Rehabilitation and Physical Medicine Clinical Management Unit of the Virgen de las Nieves University Hospital, Granada, Spain. Three samples were collected from each child, representing baseline, post-hydrotherapy and post-land-based therapy. Result: All salivary cortisol levels were within the normal range. Resting values were the highest, and both modes of therapy decreased salivary cortisol levels. There were no statistically significant differences between the two therapies. Conclusions: Both therapies appear to be useful for treating children with psychomotor developmental disorders without increasing stress during physiotherapy sessions. Although cortisol levels were slightly higher with hydrotherapy than with land-based therapy, this may be due to the small sample size.
title: Salivary Cortisol Levels after Hydrotherapy and Land-Based Therapy as a Marker of Stress in Children with Psychomotor Developmental Disorders: A Pilot Study

summary: We establish and assemble explicit algebraic, arithmetic and analytic properties of parameterized compositional inverses. We also resolve the recorded binomial-sum conjecture for A063019 and establish the exact forms of its other recorded mathematical statements. The results include a two-step effective recurrence for a cubic inverse family, Jacobi and Gegenbauer parameter-root descriptions, exact modular-Dyck first negative reversals, prime-index congruences, finite-field parity laws, Frobenius divisibility for Hankel matrices, infinite sign changes, an exact asymptotic sign-density law, strict parameter-index total positivity of order two, and boundaries for moment positivity. The proofs are carried out at the stated parameter and index ranges, using formal Lagrange inversion, finite-field algebra, orthogonal polynomials, and singularity analysis. A correspondence table for 46 named sequences and exact worked examples make the parameter specializations and the available finite verification independently reproducible. Classical inversion techniques, published single-sequence formulas, and earlier orthogonal-polynomial and moment results retain their prior attribution. The results include a two-step effective recurrence for a cubic inverse family, Jacobi and Gegenbauer parameter-root descriptions, exact modular-Dyck first negative reversals, prime-index congruences, finite-field parity laws, Frobenius divisibility for Hankel matrices, infinite sign changes, an exact asymptotic sign-density law, strict parameter-index total positivity of order two, and boundaries for moment positivity. The proofs are carried out at the stated parameter and index ranges, using formal Lagrange inversion, finite-field algebra, orthogonal polynomials, and singularity analysis. A correspondence table for 46 named sequences and exact worked examples make the parameter specializations and the available finite verification independently reproducible. Classical inversion techniques, published single-sequence formulas, and earlier orthogonal-polynomial and moment results retain their prior attribution. The independently authored verification code is made available under CC BY 4.0.
title: Structural Theorems for Parameter Families of Algebraic Series Reversions

summary: This software package contains revision-stage Python code supporting the descriptive analysis and numerical reproducibility of the manuscript entitled “Multidimensional Profiling of Heterogeneous NP-1-Associated Membrane Responses among Nine Clinical Carbapenem-Resistant Enterobacterales Isolates.” The computational workflow includes endpoint data reconstruction, technical-replicate statistics, z-score standardization, kinetic data reconstruction, missing-value handling, and numerical validation. The package operates on previously normalized supplementary datasets. Execution instructions, software dependencies, and validation records are provided to facilitate computational reproducibility and transparency.
